claim: Phytoplankton replace the iron-requiring ferredoxin electron shuttle protein with a less-efficient iron-free flavodoxin under iron-limiting conditions.
source: Phytoplankton rely on diverse mechanisms to adapt to the decreased iron bioavailability and oxidative stress-inducing conditions of today's oxygenated oceans, including replacement of the iron-requiring ferredoxin electron shuttle protein with a less-efficient iron-free flavodoxin under iron-limiting conditions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about phytoplankton adaptation mechanisms, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Diatoms transcribe flavodoxins in high-iron regions in contrast to other phytoplankton.
source: Yet, diatoms transcribe flavodoxins in high-iron regions in contrast to other phytoplankton.
evidence: This claim is supported by metatranscriptome studies cited in the manuscript (Marchetti et al., 2012; Carradec et al., 2018; Caputi et al., 2019).

claim: Two clades of flavodoxins are present within diatoms.
source: Here, we show that the two clades of flavodoxins present within diatoms exhibit a functional divergence, with only clade II flavodoxins displaying the canonical role in acclimation to iron limitation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through phylogenetic analysis and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only clade II flavodoxins display the canonical role in acclimation to iron limitation.
source: Here, we show that the two clades of flavodoxins present within diatoms exhibit a functional divergence, with only clade II flavodoxins displaying the canonical role in acclimation to iron limitation.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptional response data from multiple diatom species under iron limitation.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 knock-outs of the clade I flavodoxin from Thalassiosira pseudonana are hypersensitive to oxidative stress.
source: We created CRISPR/Cas9 knock-outs of the clade I flavodoxin from the model diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana and found that these cell lines are hypersensitive to oxidative stress, while maintaining a wild-type response to iron limitation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data showing increased cell death in KO lines exposed to H2O2.

claim: Clade I flavodoxin knock-out cell lines maintain a wild-type response to iron limitation.
source: We created CRISPR/Cas9 knock-outs of the clade I flavodoxin from the model diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana and found that these cell lines are hypersensitive to oxidative stress, while maintaining a wild-type response to iron limitation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through growth and Fv/Fm measurements under iron-limiting conditions.

claim: Clade I flavodoxin transcript abundance is regulated over the diel cycle within natural diatom communities.
source: Within natural diatom communities, clade I flavodoxin transcript abundance is regulated over the diel cycle rather than in response to iron availability, whereas clade II transcript abundances increase either in iron-limiting regions or under artificially induced iron limitation.
evidence: This is supported by metatranscriptome data from the Diel 1 cruise showing rhythmic patterns in clade I transcript abundance.

claim: Clade II flavodoxin transcript abundances increase in iron-limiting regions or under artificially induced iron limitation.
source: Within natural diatom communities, clade I flavodoxin transcript abundance is regulated over the diel cycle rather than in response to iron availability, whereas clade II transcript abundances increase either in iron-limiting regions or under artificially induced iron limitation.
evidence: This is supported by metatranscriptome data from Gradients cruises and on-deck incubation experiments.

claim: Ferredoxin is a small, soluble iron–sulfur-cluster-containing protein that accepts electrons from the stromal surface of photosystem I during oxygenic photosynthesis.
source: One of the abundant electron shuttles in phototrophs is ferredoxin (Fd), a small, soluble iron–sulfur-cluster-containing protein that accepts electrons from the stromal surface of photosystem I during oxygenic photosynthesis and facilitates transfer to acceptors involved in diverse metabolic processes (Mondal and Bruce, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ferredoxin function, supported by citation.

claim: Proteins with iron–sulfur clusters are ancient biocatalysts hypothesized to have arisen when oxygen was largely absent, and ferrous iron and sulfide were plentiful.
source: Proteins such as Fds with iron–sulfur clusters are ancient biocatalysts hypothesized to have arisen when oxygen was largely absent, and ferrous iron and sulfide were plentiful (Cammack, 1982).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Cammack, 1982.

claim: The great oxidation event occurred approximately 2.4 billion years ago.
source: During the great oxidation event approximately 2.4 billion years ago, ferrous iron became oxidized to the ferric form and rapidly precipitated either as ferric hydroxide or as insoluble complexes with anionic salts.
evidence: This is established geological knowledge.

claim: Microbial growth in aerobic habitats became limited by iron bioavailability after the great oxidation event.
source: Microbial growth in aerobic habitats thus became limited by iron bioavailability (Imlay, 2006), as found in about a third of today's oceans (Behrenfeld and Milligan, 2013; Boyd et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: About a third of today's oceans are iron-limited.
source: Microbial growth in aerobic habitats thus became limited by iron bioavailability (Imlay, 2006), as found in about a third of today's oceans (Behrenfeld and Milligan, 2013; Boyd et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to oceanographic studies.

claim: Iron-containing proteins are sensitive to damage via oxygen and reactive oxygen species.
source: Moreover, iron-containing proteins are sensitive to damage via oxygen and reactive oxygen species (ROS), and Fd is downregulated in response to oxidative stress (Singh et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on protein damage and ferredoxin regulation.

claim: Ferredoxin is downregulated in response to oxidative stress.
source: Moreover, iron-containing proteins are sensitive to damage via oxygen and reactive oxygen species (ROS), and Fd is downregulated in response to oxidative stress (Singh et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2010 and Singh et al., 2004.

claim: Contemporary marine phytoplankton may sequester up to 30–40% of their cellular iron within ferredoxin proteins.
source: Yet, contemporary marine phytoplankton (cyanobacteria and photosynthetic eukaryotes) continue to rely on Fd and may sequester up to 30–40% of their cellular iron within these proteins (Erdner, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Erdner, 1997.

claim: Photosynthetic microbes commonly replace the iron-containing ferredoxin with flavodoxin under iron-limiting conditions.
source: Under iron-limiting conditions, photosynthetic microbes commonly replace the iron-containing Fd with flavodoxin, a functional homologue (Smillie, 1965; Hutber et al., 1977; Sandmann et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to early studies on flavodoxin function.

claim: Flavodoxin uses a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as the co-factor.
source: Flavodoxin uses a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as the co-factor and is a less efficient electron shuttle, which nonetheless allows continued photosynthetic electron transport when iron is scarce (Zumft and Spiller, 1971; Yoch and Valentine, 1972).
evidence: This is established knowledge about flavodoxin structure, supported by citations.

claim: Flavodoxin is a less efficient electron shuttle than ferredoxin.
source: Flavodoxin uses a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as the co-factor and is a less efficient electron shuttle, which nonetheless allows continued photosynthetic electron transport when iron is scarce (Zumft and Spiller, 1971; Yoch and Valentine, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zumft and Spiller, 1971 and Yoch and Valentine, 1972.

claim: Flavodoxin is absent from land plants and certain coastal algal species.
source: The absence of flavodoxin from land plants and certain coastal algal species led to the premise that flavodoxin is lost from species in iron-rich environments, including terrestrial systems (Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015.

claim: Flavodoxin is induced in the cyanobacteria Synechocystis under oxidative stress.
source: However, the downregulation of Fd in response to adverse conditions (Singh et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2004) and the induction of flavodoxin in the cyanobacteria Synechocystis under oxidative stress (Jeanjean et al., 2003; Kojima et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2004) suggests additional physiological roles for flavodoxin within phytoplankton.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeanjean et al., 2003; Kojima et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2004.

claim: Expression levels of flavodoxin relative to ferredoxin have been used to evaluate whether natural communities of marine phytoplankton experience iron limitation in situ.
source: Expression levels of flavodoxin relative to Fd (inferred either from transcript or protein levels) have been used in several studies to evaluate whether natural communities of marine phytoplankton experience iron limitation in situ (Boyd et al., 1999; DiTullio et al., 2005; Erdner and Anderson, 1999; Jones, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies using this approach.

claim: Most major eukaryotic phytoplankton lineages (chlorophytes, haptophytes, and dinoflagellates) regulate flavodoxin transcript abundances in response to iron availability.
source: Metatranscriptome studies indicate that, as expected, most major eukaryotic phytoplankton lineages (chlorophytes, haptophytes, and dinoflagellates) regulate flavodoxin transcript abundances in response to iron availability, with reduced flavodoxin transcript levels in iron-replete environments (Caputi et al., 2019; Carradec et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to metatranscriptome studies.

claim: Diatom flavodoxin transcript abundances are not inversely correlated with iron availability as expected.
source: A closer examination of environmental metatranscriptomes (Marchetti et al., 2012; Carradec et al., 2018; Caputi et al., 2019) finds that diatom flavodoxin transcript abundances are not inversely correlated with iron availability as expected, and flavodoxins are often detected at high abundances under iron-replete conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to environmental metatranscriptome studies.

claim: Ferredoxin is encoded on the plastid genomes of some diatoms.
source: Although direct comparisons between environmental flavodoxin and Fd transcript abundances are complicated by the fact that Fd is encoded on the plastid genomes of some diatoms (Groussman et al., 2015; Gueneau et al., 1998; Lommer et al., 2010; Oudot-Le Secq et al., 2007; Roy et al., 2020), diatoms appear to regulate the transcription of flavodoxin differently compared to other phytoplankton.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on diatom plastid genomes.

claim: Flavodoxin diverged into two distinct phylogenetic clades in model diatoms.
source: A potential explanation for the distinctive flavodoxin transcriptional patterns of natural communities of diatoms comes from the discovery in a few model diatoms that flavodoxin diverged into two distinct phylogenetic clades with only those flavodoxins from clade II induced upon iron limitation, suggesting that clade I flavodoxins may play a different role within these species (Whitney et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Whitney et al., 2011.

claim: In three model diatoms that encode both clade I and clade II flavodoxins, only the clade II flavodoxins were significantly induced upon iron limitation.
source: We supplemented this work by examining publicly available transcript data and found that in the three model diatoms that encode both clade I and clade II flavodoxins, only the clade II flavodoxins were significantly induced upon iron limitation (Graff van Creveld et al., 2016; Lommer et al., 2012; Mock et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2016; summed in Supplementary file 1a), reiterating the potential for different functional roles of these proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple transcriptome studies and data presented in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: The flavodoxin domain was detected in 1191 flavodoxin genes from publicly available genomes and transcriptomes of over 500 marine protists, bacteria, and archaea.
source: The flavodoxin domain was detected in 1191 flavodoxin genes (Supplementary file 2; supplementary fasta file 2) and included 332 genes that clustered with known photosynthetic flavodoxin proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, black labels); the remaining sequences displayed similarity to a diverse and distant clade of non-photosynthesis-related proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, red labels).
evidence: This is based on HMM search results and phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 332 flavodoxin genes clustered with known photosynthetic flavodoxin proteins.
source: The flavodoxin domain was detected in 1191 flavodoxin genes (Supplementary file 2; supplementary fasta file 2) and included 332 genes that clustered with known photosynthetic flavodoxin proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, black labels); the remaining sequences displayed similarity to a diverse and distant clade of non-photosynthesis-related proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, red labels).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Photosynthesis-associated flavodoxins segregate into four clades.
source: The presumed photosynthesis-associated flavodoxins segregate into four clades (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Two clades of photosynthetic flavodoxins were composed of flavodoxins from green algae.
source: Two clades were composed of photosynthetic flavodoxins from green algae, one that grouped with gamma-proteobacteria (highlighted in pink, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and another that grouped with cyanobacteria and dinoflagellates (highlighted in green, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Labeled Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus flavodoxins were previously shown to be induced in response to iron limitation.
source: Within these clusters, the labeled Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus flavodoxins were previously shown to be induced in response to iron limitation (Kashtan et al., 2014; Mackey et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 2011; Yousef et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on cyanobacterial flavodoxin induction.

claim: Clade I and II flavodoxins were detected exclusively in eukaryotic algae originally derived from a secondary endosymbiosis of a red alga.
source: Clade I and II flavodoxins, as originally identified by Whitney et al., 2011, were detected exclusively in eukaryotic algae originally derived from a secondary endosymbiosis of a red alga (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree and supported by citation to Whitney et al., 2011.

claim: Clade I flavodoxins were detected in stramenopiles and two dinoflagellates (Durinskia baltica and Kryptoperidinium foliaceum).
source: Clade I flavodoxins were detected in stramenopiles (highlighted in orange, Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and two dinoflagellates (Durinskia baltica and Kryptoperidinium foliaceum).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both Durinskia baltica and Kryptoperidinium foliaceum express proteins originating from their diatom endosymbionts.
source: Both dinoflagellates express proteins originating from their diatom endosymbionts (Hehenberger et al., 2016; Imanian et al., 2010; Imanian and Keeling, 2007; Yamada et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on dinoflagellate endosymbionts.

claim: None of the previously tested clade I flavodoxin genes transcriptionally respond to iron limiting growth conditions.
source: None of the previously tested clade I flavodoxin genes transcriptionally respond to iron limiting growth conditions (stars, Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and documented in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Clade II flavodoxins are phylogenetically more diverse than clade I flavodoxins.
source: Clade II flavodoxins are phylogenetically more diverse than clade I flavodoxins and consist of sequences from diatoms, non-diatom stramenopiles, haptophytes, and dinoflagellates (Karenia brevis and Karlodinium micrum) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A Phaeocystis flavodoxin was experimentally induced under iron limitation.
source: The base of clade II is defined here by a cluster of haptophyte sequences that includes a Phaeocystis flavodoxin (labeled) experimentally induced under iron limitation (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2019.

claim: Known diatom iron-limitation-responsive flavodoxins all cluster within clade II.
source: Known diatom iron-limitation-responsive flavodoxins all cluster within clade II (Supplementary file 1a), consistent with a functional divergence between clade I and clade II flavodoxins within the stramenopiles.
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1a and shown in phylogenetic trees.

claim: Flavodoxins from both clades appear to be similarly distributed amongst open ocean and coastal isolates.
source: Flavodoxins from both clades appear to be similarly distributed amongst open ocean and coastal isolates, with no evidence that clade II flavodoxins are retained only in species isolated from low-iron environments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and documented in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Diatom clade I flavodoxins from pennate and centric diatoms form a tight cluster with high bootstrap support.
source: Diatom clade I flavodoxins from pennate and centric diatoms form a tight cluster with high bootstrap support (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), with multiple copies detected in a subset of species (Supplementary file 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Multiple copies of clade I flavodoxins were detected in a subset of diatom species.
source: Diatom clade I flavodoxins from pennate and centric diatoms form a tight cluster with high bootstrap support (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), with multiple copies detected in a subset of species (Supplementary file 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1b and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Many examined taxa encode both clade I and clade II flavodoxins.
source: Many examined taxa encode both clade I and clade II flavodoxins.
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic analysis and documented in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: About half of the examined taxa appear to encode a flavodoxin from only one clade.
source: About half of the taxa appear to encode a flavodoxin from only one clade (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), although this absence may reflect culture conditions rather than absence from their respective genomes as most available sequence data are derived from transcriptomes (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and documented in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The absence of clade I flavodoxin sequences appears more common in stramenopiles that are more distantly related to diatoms.
source: Nonetheless, the absence of clade I flavodoxin sequences appears more common in stramenopiles that are more distantly related to diatoms, such as Phaeomonas (Pinguiophyceae; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), while stramenopiles more closely related to diatoms, such as members of Pelagophyceae and Dictyochophyceae, commonly encode both clade I and clade II flavodoxins (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and documented in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Amino acid side chains that form hydrogen bonds with the FMN are conserved between clade I and clade II flavodoxins.
source: As expected, amino acid side chains that form hydrogen bonds with the FMN (underlined in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) are conserved between the two clades.
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Clade I and clade II flavodoxin sequences differ from each other at amino acids 57 and 103.
source: The clade I and clade II flavodoxin sequences differ from each other at amino acids 57 and 103 (numbered according to C. crispus sequence, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: At amino acid 57, the dominant amino acid is asparagine (N) in C. crispus and clade I proteins, and histidine (H) in clade II proteins.
source: At amino acid 57, the dominant amino acid is asparagine (N) in C. crispus and clade I proteins, and histidine (H) in clade II proteins.
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: At amino acid 103, the dominant amino acid is cysteine (C) in C. crispus and clade II proteins, and alanine (A) in clade I proteins.
source: At amino acid 103, the dominant amino acid is cysteine (C) in C. crispus and clade II proteins, and alanine (A) in clade I proteins.
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both distinguishing amino acid changes occur near the FMN-binding tryptophan and tyrosine.
source: Both distinguishing amino acid changes occur near the FMN-binding tryptophan and tyrosine (W56, Y98, indicated with asterisks in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), consistent with distinct functions for the two flavodoxins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and represents an inference about functional significance.

claim: Desferrioxamine B (DFB) was used to enhance short-term iron limitation in diatom experiments.
source: In order to facilitate screening of multiple diatoms for whether they transcribed clade I and II flavodoxins in response to iron limitation, we used the strong iron-chelator desferrioxamine B (DFB) and enhanced short-term iron limitation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: Oxidative stress was induced by the lowest lethal dose of H2O2 (200–250 µM).
source: Oxidative stress was induced by the lowest lethal dose of H2O2 (200–250 µM), as a similar treatment was shown to be representative of other, environmentally relevant form of oxidative stressors in T. pseudonana and Phaeodactylum (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Mizrachi et al., 2019; Volpert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, supported by citations.

claim: The three experimental conditions (control, iron limitation, oxidative stress) elicited distinct overall transcriptional responses in the five diatom species.
source: The three conditions elicited distinct overall transcriptional responses in the five diatom species as seen in multidimensional scaling (MDS) plots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the MDS plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: T. oceanica transcribed two isoforms of clade II flavodoxins.
source: Cylindrotheca and T. oceanica transcribed both clade I and II flavodoxins; T. oceanica transcribed two isoforms of clade II flavodoxins (labeled here A, B, Figure 2B); T. pseudonana, Chaetoceros, and Amphora transcribed only clade I flavodoxins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B based on transcriptome data.

claim: T. pseudonana, Chaetoceros, and Amphora transcribed only clade I flavodoxins.
source: Cylindrotheca and T. oceanica transcribed both clade I and II flavodoxins; T. oceanica transcribed two isoforms of clade II flavodoxins (labeled here A, B, Figure 2B); T. pseudonana, Chaetoceros, and Amphora transcribed only clade I flavodoxins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 based on transcriptome data.

claim: The transcription levels of clade II genes from T. oceanica (clade II-A) and Cylindrotheca were significantly elevated in response to iron limitation (5.3- and 9.5-fold change, respectively, FDR <0.01).
source: The transcription levels of clade II genes from T. oceanica (clade II-A) and Cylindrotheca were significantly elevated in response to iron limitation (5.3- and 9.5-fold change, respectively, false discovery rate [FDR] <0.01, Figure 2B), whereas the clade I genes in these diatoms did not display a significant change in transcript abundance either after exposure to H2O2 or under iron limitation (FDR = 1, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome data shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: The clade I genes in T. oceanica and Cylindrotheca did not display a significant change in transcript abundance either after exposure to H2O2 or under iron limitation (FDR = 1).
source: The transcription levels of clade II genes from T. oceanica (clade II-A) and Cylindrotheca were significantly elevated in response to iron limitation (5.3- and 9.5-fold change, respectively, false discovery rate [FDR] <0.01, Figure 2B), whereas the clade I genes in these diatoms did not display a significant change in transcript abundance either after exposure to H2O2 or under iron limitation (FDR = 1, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: The T. oceanica clade II-B gene transcript levels were not responsive to either iron limitation or H2O2 treatment.
source: The T. oceanica clade II-B gene transcript levels were not responsive to either treatment (Figure 1B), in agreement with previous results (Supplementary file 1a, Lommer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome data shown in Figure 2B and supported by citation to Lommer et al., 2012.

claim: The transcribed clade I flavodoxins of T. pseudonana, Chaetoceros, and Amphora were elevated under iron limitation (3.2-, 1.5-, and 9.9-fold change, respectively, FDR < 0.01).
source: The transcribed clade I flavodoxins of T. pseudonana, Chaetoceros, and Amphora were elevated under iron limitation (3.2-, 1.5-, and 9.9-fold change, respectively, FDR < 0.01, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Clade I flavodoxins are induced in iron limitation only when clade II flavodoxins are absent.
source: These diatoms encode only a clade I flavodoxin, suggesting that clade I flavodoxins are induced in iron limitation only when clade II flavodoxins are absent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only diatoms lacking clade II show clade I induction under iron limitation.

claim: Only the T. pseudonana clade I flavodoxin gene was significantly differentially transcribed in response to H2O2 treatment (2.4-fold increase, FDR < 0.01).
source: Only the T. pseudonana clade I flavodoxin gene was significantly differentially transcribed in response to H2O2 treatment (2.4-fold increase, FDR < 0.01, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Three independent clade I flavodoxin knock-out lines were generated in T. pseudonana using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 was used to generate three independent KO lines, each with deleted FMN-binding sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method and results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell growth, Fv/Fm, and the final carrying capacity were not significantly different between WT and KO cells under iron-replete growth conditions.
source: Cell growth, Fv/Fm, and the final carrying capacity were not significantly different between WT and KO cells under iron-replete growth conditions (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Cell counts were similar between WT and KO lines, reaching about 3 million cells per ml at day 12 (WT 3.04±0.25, KO 2.93±0.11).
source: Cell counts were similar between WT and KO lines, reaching about 3 million cells per ml at day 12 (WT 3.04±0.25, KO 2.93±0.11, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Photosynthetic efficiency was similar between WT and KO cells (0.64±0.016, 0.63±0.040, respectively, at day 1).
source: Photosynthetic efficiency was also similar between WT and KO cells (0.64±0.016, 0.63±0.040, respectively, at day 1, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The WT and KO lines displayed comparable reductions in cell division and Fv/Fm under iron limitation.
source: The WT and KO lines displayed comparable reductions in cell division and Fv/Fm under iron limitation and after ~3 d, reached a maximum of about 400,000 cells per ml (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), and decreased in Fv/Fm from 0.63±0.016 (all cell lines in replete conditions) to 0.57±0.016 (KO lines) or 0.57±0.004 (WT lines) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Wild-type T. pseudonana cells do not replace their iron-requiring ferredoxin with flavodoxin during acclimation to low iron.
source: Thus, both wild-type and KO T. pseudonana lines respond poorly to iron-limiting conditions, which suggests that wild-type cells do not replace their iron-requiring Fd with flavodoxin during acclimation to low iron.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that WT and KO lines respond similarly to iron limitation.

claim: Exposure to 100 µM H2O2 killed ~73% of WT cells after 24 hr.
source: Exposure to 100 µM H2O2 killed ~73% of WT cells after 24 hr.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Exposure of KO cells to 100 µM H2O2 resulted in the death of ~100% of the KO cells after 24 hr.
source: In contrast, exposure of KO cells to the same dose of H2O2 resulted in the death of ~100% of the KO cells after 24 hr, comparable to what was seen when WT cells were exposed to twice the amount of H2O2 (200 µM).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The hypersensitivity of KO lines to H2O2 indicates that clade I flavodoxins play a role in the oxidative stress response.
source: The hypersensitivity of KO lines to H2O2 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I) indicates that clade I flavodoxins play a role in the oxidative stress response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased sensitivity of KO lines to H2O2.

claim: A total of 120 eukaryotic surface-water metatranscriptomes were sampled during three research cruises in the North Pacific Ocean.
source: To expand our analysis beyond laboratory studies and explore the potential roles of clade I and clade II flavodoxins in natural communities, we interrogated a total of 120 eukaryotic surface-water metatranscriptomes sampled during three research cruises in the North Pacific Ocean: Gradients 1 cruise (April/May 2016) transited south/north along ~158°W, from 21°N to 38°N (10 stations, triplicates); Gradients 2 cruise (May/June 2017) transited south/north along ~158°W, from 24°N to 42.5°N (10 stations, triplicates), and a diel sampling cruise (July/August 2015) was conducted in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (NPSG), at ~156.5°W, 24.5°N near station ALOHA (24 times points, duplicates); an on-deck nutrient-addition experiment was conducted on Gradients 2 at 37°N, 158°W (incubations: four conditions, triplicates) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling design and locations.

claim: Contigs for the two flavodoxin clades were detected in metatranscriptomes from all three expeditions.
source: Contigs for the two flavodoxin clades were detected in metatranscriptomes from all three expeditions, with a greater number and phylogenetic diversity of clade II flavodoxin contigs, particularly along the Gradients 1 and 2 transects (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A greater number and phylogenetic diversity of clade II flavodoxin contigs were detected, particularly along the Gradients 1 and 2 transects.
source: Contigs for the two flavodoxin clades were detected in metatranscriptomes from all three expeditions, with a greater number and phylogenetic diversity of clade II flavodoxin contigs, particularly along the Gradients 1 and 2 transects (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The majority of environmental clade II flavodoxins were most closely related to the reference sequence of the radial centric diatom Chaetoceros dichaeta.
source: The majority of environmental clade II flavodoxins were most closely related to the reference sequence of the radial centric diatom Chaetoceros dichaeta, originally isolated from the South Atlantic; additional clade II contigs were distributed amongst 11 other diatom genera (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic placement analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within the non-diatom stramenopiles, a majority of clade II flavodoxin contigs were assigned to Dictyocha and Florenciella.
source: Within the non-diatom stramenopiles, a majority of clade II flavodoxin contigs were assigned to Dictyocha and Florenciella, with additional contigs distributed amongst five other genera (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic placement analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The clade I flavodoxins were assigned primarily to Fistulifera solaris, a small pennate diatom similar to those dominating the diatom population in this area.
source: The clade I flavodoxins were assigned primarily to Fistulifera solaris, a small pennate diatom similar to those dominating the diatom population in this area (Dore et al., 2008; Villareal et al., 2012); additional clade I contigs were assigned to three other reference diatoms, including C. dichaeta, and two non-diatom stramenopiles (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic placement analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations supporting the dominance of similar diatoms.

claim: Community composition, nutrient availability, and flavodoxin transcriptional patterns varied spatially along the Gradients 1 and 2 south/north transects.
source: Community composition, nutrient availability (Gradoville et al., 2020; Juranek et al., 2020; Lambert et al., 2022; Park et al., 2022; Pinedo-González et al., 2020), and flavodoxin transcriptional patterns (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1d) varied spatially along the Gradients 1 and 2 south/north transects.
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome and nutrient data, supported by multiple citations.

claim: On Gradients 1, iron (Fe) and nitrate (N) displayed the expected opposing concentration patterns with increasing N and decreasing Fe concentrations north of the NPSG.
source: On Gradients 1, iron (Fe) and nitrate (N) displayed the expected opposing concentration patterns with increasing N and decreasing Fe concentrations north of the NPSG, resulting in low N/Fe (~0.01 μM/nM) within the NPSG and 3–4 orders of magnitude higher N/Fe (~10–100 μM/nM) within the transition zone and further north (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on nutrient measurements shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: On Gradients 2, Fe increased within the transition zone due to increased dust deposition.
source: In contrast, on Gradients 2, Fe increased within the transition zone due to increased dust deposition (Pinedo-González et al., 2020), resulting in a relatively low N/Fe (<10 μM/nM) throughout the transition zone up to ~40°N (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is based on nutrient measurements shown in Figure 5E and F, with citation to Pinedo-González et al., 2020.

claim: Clade I flavodoxin transcripts were detected for two genera, Fistulifera and Dactyliosolen.
source: Clade I flavodoxin transcripts were detected for two genera, Fistulifera and Dactyliosolen, and the relative abundances of these transcripts were higher within the NPSG where N/Fe ratio remained <1 (µM/nM) for both cruises (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: The relative abundances of clade I flavodoxin transcripts were higher within the NPSG where N/Fe ratio remained <1 (µM/nM) for both cruises.
source: Clade I flavodoxin transcripts were detected for two genera, Fistulifera and Dactyliosolen, and the relative abundances of these transcripts were higher within the NPSG where N/Fe ratio remained <1 (µM/nM) for both cruises (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: On Gradients 1, relative clade II flavodoxin transcript abundances increased within the transition zone, peaking at 33°N where the N/Fe ratio reached >37 (µM/nM).
source: On Gradients 1, relative clade II flavodoxin transcript abundances increased within the transition zone, peaking at 33°N where the N/Fe ratio reached >37 (µM/nM), for all detected genera except Chaetoceros, which displayed the highest relative transcript abundances at 37°N, the most northern station of this transect (Figure 5A, C and D).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome and nutrient data shown in Figure 5A, C and D.

claim: Chaetoceros displayed the highest relative clade II transcript abundances at 37°N on Gradients 1, the most northern station of this transect.
source: On Gradients 1, relative clade II flavodoxin transcript abundances increased within the transition zone, peaking at 33°N where the N/Fe ratio reached >37 (µM/nM), for all detected genera except Chaetoceros, which displayed the highest relative transcript abundances at 37°N, the most northern station of this transect (Figure 5A, C and D).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data shown in Figure 5A, C and D.

claim: On Gradients 2, transcript abundances for 4 of 10 detected genera did not peak until 40°N, the station at which N/Fe first reached >6 μM/nM.
source: Consistent with the higher Fe concentrations detected on Gradients 2 (Park et al., 2022; Pinedo-González et al., 2020), relative clade II transcript abundance did not undergo as great an increase within the transition zone as seen during the Gradients I cruise. Instead, transcript abundances for 4 of 10 detected genera did not peak until 40°N, the station at which N/Fe first reached >6 μM/nM (Figure 5B, E and F).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome and nutrient data shown in Figure 5B, E and F.

claim: Clade II flavodoxins are expressed by diverse genera specifically under relatively high-nitrate, low-iron conditions.
source: These results indicate that clade II flavodoxins are expressed by diverse genera specifically under relatively high-nitrate, low-iron conditions, whereas clade I flavodoxin transcription is restricted to a few diatom genera in oligotrophic, non-iron-limiting conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial patterns of flavodoxin transcription along the transects.

claim: Clade I flavodoxin transcription is restricted to a few diatom genera in oligotrophic, non-iron-limiting conditions.
source: These results indicate that clade II flavodoxins are expressed by diverse genera specifically under relatively high-nitrate, low-iron conditions, whereas clade I flavodoxin transcription is restricted to a few diatom genera in oligotrophic, non-iron-limiting conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial patterns of flavodoxin transcription along the transects.

claim: On-deck incubation experiments were conducted on Gradients 2 using trace-metal clean seawater collected from 37°N, 158°W where the in situ N/Fe ratio was 0.24 (µM/nM).
source: To determine how North Pacific diatom genera at a given location respond to changes in N/Fe, we conducted on-deck incubation experiments on Gradients 2 using trace-metal clean seawater collected from 37°N, 158°W where the in situ N/Fe ratio was 0.24 (µM/nM, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and conditions.

claim: Clade I flavodoxins transcripts were low in both in situ samples (T = 0) and in the experimental treatments (T = 4 d) at 37°N.
source: Clade I flavodoxins transcripts were low in both in situ samples (T = 0) and in the experimental treatments (T = 4 d) (37°N Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1d) with both nutrient amendment conditions (Fe or N+P) resulting in a reduction in relative transcript abundances assigned to Chaetoceros and Dactyliosolen (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data from the incubation experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Both nutrient amendment conditions (Fe or N+P) resulted in a reduction in relative clade I transcript abundances assigned to Chaetoceros and Dactyliosolen.
source: Clade I flavodoxins transcripts were low in both in situ samples (T = 0) and in the experimental treatments (T = 4 d) (37°N Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1d) with both nutrient amendment conditions (Fe or N+P) resulting in a reduction in relative transcript abundances assigned to Chaetoceros and Dactyliosolen (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data from the incubation experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Relative clade II transcript abundances increased significantly in the N+P amendment treatment compared to both the controls and the Fe amendment in all genera except Chaetoceros, Proboscia, and Pseudo-nitzschia.
source: In contrast, relative clade II transcript abundances increased significantly in the N+P amendment treatment compared to both the controls and the Fe amendment in all genera except Chaetoceros, Proboscia, and Pseudo-nitzschia (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data from the incubation experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Proboscia displayed the highest relative clade II transcript abundances in situ (T = 0).
source: Proboscia displayed the highest relative transcript abundances in situ (T = 0) and Chaetoceros and Pseudo-nitzschia displayed the highest relative transcript abundances in the control.
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data from the incubation experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Chaetoceros and Pseudo-nitzschia displayed the highest relative clade II transcript abundances in the control.
source: Proboscia displayed the highest relative transcript abundances in situ (T = 0) and Chaetoceros and Pseudo-nitzschia displayed the highest relative transcript abundances in the control.
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data from the incubation experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Diatoms can respond to iron limitation by upregulating transcription of clade II flavodoxins.
source: Together, these results indicate that diatoms can respond to iron limitation by upregulating transcription of clade II flavodoxins, which supports the inference that the relatively low abundance of clade II transcripts detected in situ at 37°N reflected iron-replete conditions at the time of sampling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incubation experiment results.

claim: The relatively low abundance of clade II transcripts detected in situ at 37°N reflected iron-replete conditions at the time of sampling.
source: Together, these results indicate that diatoms can respond to iron limitation by upregulating transcription of clade II flavodoxins, which supports the inference that the relatively low abundance of clade II transcripts detected in situ at 37°N reflected iron-replete conditions at the time of sampling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incubation experiment results.

claim: Metatranscriptomes were collected in duplicate every 4 hr for 4 d within the NPSG during the Diel 1 cruise.
source: To further explore a potential role for clade I flavodoxins, we examined transcriptional patterns of clade I and clade II flavodoxins in metatranscriptomes collected in duplicate every 4 hr for 4 d within the NPSG (Diel 1 cruise, Wilson et al., 2017), a low-nitrogen, high-light environment.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling design, supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2017.

claim: Each day during the Diel 1 cruise, the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) reached ~2000 µmol photons·m–2·s–1.
source: Each day the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) reached ~2000 µmol photons·m–2·s–1 (Coesel et al., 2021), conditions expected to enhance oxidative stress.
evidence: This is based on PAR measurements, supported by citation to Coesel et al., 2021.

claim: Clade II transcript abundances were low throughout the diel cycle during the Diel 1 cruise.
source: Clade II transcript abundances were low throughout the diel cycle (Figure 5H), in agreement with the low transcript levels detected at similar latitudes along the Gradients transects (~24°N, Figure 5A and B) representative of the non-iron-limiting conditions at these stations.
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Clade I flavodoxins exhibited a clear diel pattern in transcript abundance during the Diel 1 cruise.
source: In contrast, clade I flavodoxins exhibited a clear diel pattern in transcript abundance.
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Most clade I flavodoxin contigs during the Diel 1 cruise were assigned to F. solaris.
source: Most contigs were assigned to F. solaris, and 13 out of 19 contigs had a significant peak in transcript abundance at 6 AM (RAIN analysis, BH correlation <0.05) that then decreased gradually throughout the day and reached a minimum at dusk.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic placement and RAIN analysis of metatranscriptome data.

claim: 13 out of 19 clade I flavodoxin contigs had a significant peak in transcript abundance at 6 AM (RAIN analysis, BH correlation <0.05).
source: Most contigs were assigned to F. solaris, and 13 out of 19 contigs had a significant peak in transcript abundance at 6 AM (RAIN analysis, BH correlation <0.05) that then decreased gradually throughout the day and reached a minimum at dusk.
evidence: This is based on RAIN analysis of metatranscriptome data.

claim: The increase in clade I transcript abundances during the night beginning at ~10 PM to 2 AM suggests a diel-regulated anticipation of the high light exposure after dawn.
source: The increase in clade I transcript abundances during the night beginning at ~10 PM to 2 AM suggests a diel-regulated anticipation of the high light exposure after dawn.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diel pattern of clade I transcript abundance.

claim: Both ferredoxin and flavodoxin were presumably present in the cyanobacteria engulfed during the primary endosymbiosis that gave rise to the plastids of the green, red, and glaucophyte algae.
source: Both ferredoxin and flavodoxin were presumably present in the cyanobacteria engulfed during the primary endosymbiosis that gave rise to the plastids of the green, red, and glaucophyte algae (Campbell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2019.

claim: During the subsequent secondary endosymbiosis of a red alga, ferredoxin and flavodoxin were transferred to stramenopile, dinoflagellate, and haptophyte lineages.
source: During the subsequent secondary endosymbiosis of a red alga, these proteins were transferred to stramenopile, dinoflagellate, and haptophyte lineages, which together dominate carbon flux in contemporary global oceans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about secondary endosymbiosis and protein transfer.

claim: Stramenopile, dinoflagellate, and haptophyte lineages together dominate carbon flux in contemporary global oceans.
source: During the subsequent secondary endosymbiosis of a red alga, these proteins were transferred to stramenopile, dinoflagellate, and haptophyte lineages, which together dominate carbon flux in contemporary global oceans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ecological importance of these lineages.

claim: The complex evolutionary history of flavodoxin has resulted in distributions scattered across all domains of life.
source: The complex evolutionary history of flavodoxin has resulted in distributions scattered across all domains of life, a pattern hypothesized to reflect both multiple horizontal gene transfers and gene loss in organisms that evolved in iron-rich environments (Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015; Pierella Karlusich and Carrillo, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015 and Pierella Karlusich and Carrillo, 2017.

claim: The scattered distribution of flavodoxin is hypothesized to reflect both multiple horizontal gene transfers and gene loss in organisms that evolved in iron-rich environments.
source: The complex evolutionary history of flavodoxin has resulted in distributions scattered across all domains of life, a pattern hypothesized to reflect both multiple horizontal gene transfers and gene loss in organisms that evolved in iron-rich environments (Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015; Pierella Karlusich and Carrillo, 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015 and Pierella Karlusich and Carrillo, 2017.

claim: Responsiveness to iron limitation by both marine cyanobacterial and green algal flavodoxins supports the proposition that iron availability is a strong selective pressure on retention of flavodoxin within the genomes of these organisms.
source: Responsiveness to iron limitation by both marine cyanobacterial and green algal flavodoxins supports the proposition that iron availability is a strong selective pressure on retention of flavodoxin within the genomes of these organisms (Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Pierella Karlusich et al., 2015.

claim: The distribution of clade II flavodoxins across stramenopiles lineages appears unrelated to contemporary iron conditions.
source: Clade II flavodoxins from model organisms display responsiveness to iron limitation, exhibiting the expected canonical replacement of ferredoxin by flavodoxin under iron-limiting conditions. Yet, the distribution of clade II flavodoxins across stramenopiles lineages appears unrelated to contemporary iron conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution analysis.

claim: Clade I flavodoxins are restricted to stramenopiles, apparently differentiated in the Diatomista after their divergence from the Chrysista.
source: Clade I flavodoxins are restricted to stramenopiles, apparently differentiated in the Diatomista after their divergence from the Chrysista (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Clade I flavodoxins appear to have been retained across diverse diatoms and are often present in multiple copies, regardless of whether the species was originally isolated from the iron-poor open ocean or the iron-rich coastal environment.
source: Clade I flavodoxins appear to have been retained across diverse diatoms and are often present in multiple copies, regardless of whether the species was originally isolated from the iron-poor open ocean or the iron-rich coastal environment suggesting alternative selective pressures.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic distribution analysis and suggests alternative selective pressures.

claim: In Escherichia coli, overexpression of endogenous flavodoxin resulted in enhanced resistance to oxidative stress.
source: However, in Escherichia coli, overexpression of endogenous flavodoxin resulted in enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Zheng et al., 1999), and ectopic expression of cyanobacterial flavodoxin in land plants leads to enhanced tolerance to a broad range of stresses, including oxidative stress (Blanco et al., 2011; Ceccoli et al., 2011; Mayta et al., 2019; Tognetti et al., 2006; Zurbriggen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zheng et al., 1999.

claim: Ectopic expression of cyanobacterial flavodoxin in land plants leads to enhanced tolerance to a broad range of stresses, including oxidative stress.
source: However, in Escherichia coli, overexpression of endogenous flavodoxin resulted in enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Zheng et al., 1999), and ectopic expression of cyanobacterial flavodoxin in land plants leads to enhanced tolerance to a broad range of stresses, including oxidative stress (Blanco et al., 2011; Ceccoli et al., 2011; Mayta et al., 2019; Tognetti et al., 2006; Zurbriggen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on flavodoxin expression in plants.

claim: In those diatoms with only clade I flavodoxins, ferredoxin replacement as a means of reducing iron requirements may play a less important role in acclimation to low-iron conditions.
source: In those diatoms that lack clade II flavodoxin, the clade I flavodoxin is also induced by iron limitation, although at two orders of magnitude lower transcript abundances (Figure 2B and C, Supplementary file 1a). This suggests that in those diatoms with only clade I flavodoxins, Fd replacement as a means of reducing iron requirements may play a less important role in acclimation to low-iron conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low transcript abundances of clade I flavodoxins under iron limitation.

claim: Clade I flavodoxins are distinguished from the clade II flavodoxins by replacement of cysteine with alanine at residue 103.
source: Further support for the role of clade I flavodoxin during oxidative stress comes from our observation that the clade I flavodoxins are distinguished from the clade II flavodoxins by replacement of cysteine with alanine at residue 103 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cysteines are susceptible to oxidation under oxidative stress.
source: Cysteines are susceptible to oxidation under oxidative stress (D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007), which would be expected to inactivate the clade II protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007.

claim: Oxidation of cysteine would be expected to inactivate the clade II flavodoxin protein.
source: Cysteines are susceptible to oxidation under oxidative stress (D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007), which would be expected to inactivate the clade II protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the susceptibility of cysteine to oxidation.

claim: The clade I gene is transcribed at orders of magnitude lower levels than the clade II gene, in cultures and in the North Pacific.
source: The observation that the clade I gene is transcribed at orders of magnitude lower levels than the clade II gene, in cultures and in the North Pacific, suggests either that different transcriptional controls may regulate clade I flavodoxin transcript accumulation within a cell or that oxidative stress may deplete a smaller fraction of the Fd pool compared to iron deprivation.
evidence: This is based on transcript abundance data from laboratory and environmental samples.

claim: Low clade I transcript abundances in bulk measurements may reflect the previously observed heterogeneity in the response of individual cells to H2O2 exposure.
source: Alternatively, low clade I transcript abundances in our bulk measurements may reflect the previously observed heterogeneity in the response of individual cells to H2O2 exposure (Mizrachi et al., 2019), our means of eliciting oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Mizrachi et al., 2019.

claim: Clade II flavodoxins in diatoms in the wild are transcribed in environments where nitrate assimilation is decreased due to iron limitation, defined here by elevated N/Fe (>4 μM N/nM Fe).
source: Our metatranscriptomes studies of eukaryotic phytoplankton communities identified both general patterns in transcriptional profiles of the clade I and II flavodoxin genes and highlighted specific responses of different diatoms. Clade II flavodoxins in diatoms in the wild are transcribed in environments where nitrate assimilation is decreased due to iron limitation, defined here by elevated N/Fe (>4 μM N/nM Fe).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis from the Gradients cruises.

claim: The environmental Chaetoceros transcribed clade II flavodoxin exclusively at putative iron-limiting stations.
source: The environmental Chaetoceros transcribed clade II flavodoxin exclusively at putative iron-limiting stations, despite detection of this genus at other non-iron-limiting stations.
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis from the Gradients cruises.

claim: Two environmental diatom genera, Pseudo-nitzschia and Fragilariopsis, were both numerically abundant based on their total transcript abundances.
source: In contrast, two other environmental diatom genera, Pseudo-nitzschia and Fragilariopsis, were both numerically abundant based on their total transcript abundances (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and yet the clade II transcript abundance for these two species remained relatively low throughout both transects, suggesting that these species were not experiencing iron limitation at the time of sampling.
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The clade II transcript abundance for Pseudo-nitzschia and Fragilariopsis remained relatively low throughout both transects, suggesting that these species were not experiencing iron limitation at the time of sampling.
source: In contrast, two other environmental diatom genera, Pseudo-nitzschia and Fragilariopsis, were both numerically abundant based on their total transcript abundances (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and yet the clade II transcript abundance for these two species remained relatively low throughout both transects, suggesting that these species were not experiencing iron limitation at the time of sampling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low clade II transcript abundances.

claim: The pelagophyte Pelagomonas was abundant across the transects and yet also transcribed clade II at relatively low levels.
source: Similarly, the pelagophyte Pelagomonas was also abundant across the transects and yet also transcribed clade II at relatively low levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on metatranscriptome analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Several of the detected Chaetoceros species encode clade I flavodoxins.
source: Importantly, several of the detected Chaetoceros species encode clade I flavodoxins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which were either detected at relatively low levels or not detected at all along the transects, indicating the specificity of transcription of the two flavodoxin clades in response to environmental conditions.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic placement analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NPSG is an iron-replete, high-light environment.
source: The NPSG is an iron-replete, high-light environment, condition that enhances oxidative stress and may thus compromise Fd functionality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NPSG environment.

claim: High-light conditions enhance oxidative stress and may thus compromise ferredoxin functionality.
source: The NPSG is an iron-replete, high-light environment, condition that enhances oxidative stress and may thus compromise Fd functionality.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about oxidative stress.

claim: Phaeodactylum tricornutum clade I flavodoxin (Phatr3_J13706) expression peaked just before and after dusk.
source: Interestingly, genome-wide transcriptomic profiles of two model diatoms over the diel cycle also suggest a diel rhythm to clade I flavodoxins transcript abundance. Phaeodactylum tricornutum clade I flavodoxin (Phatr3_J13706) expression peaked just before and after dusk (Smith et al., 2016), and the benthic diatom Seminavis robusta induced the clade I flavodoxins (sro1985_g309400, sro668_g166050) before dusk (Bilcke et al., 2021; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2016.

claim: The benthic diatom Seminavis robusta induced the clade I flavodoxins (sro1985_g309400, sro668_g166050) before dusk.
source: Interestingly, genome-wide transcriptomic profiles of two model diatoms over the diel cycle also suggest a diel rhythm to clade I flavodoxins transcript abundance. Phaeodactylum tricornutum clade I flavodoxin (Phatr3_J13706) expression peaked just before and after dusk (Smith et al., 2016), and the benthic diatom Seminavis robusta induced the clade I flavodoxins (sro1985_g309400, sro668_g166050) before dusk (Bilcke et al., 2021; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bilcke et al., 2021.

claim: The diel rhythmicity of clade I flavodoxins in both laboratory studies with model diatoms, as well as the diel rhythmicity in natural diatom communities, emphasizes the potential circadian regulation of this protein in anticipation of the dawn and photosynthetic-related oxidative stress.
source: The diel rhythmicity of clade I flavodoxins in both laboratory studies with model diatoms, as well as the diel rhythmicity in natural diatom communities, emphasizes the potential circadian regulation of this protein in anticipation of the dawn and photosynthetic-related oxidative stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed diel patterns in multiple datasets.

claim: Not all flavodoxins are responsive to low-iron concentrations.
source: Here we show that not all flavodoxins are responsive to low-iron concentrations, and that a subset of flavodoxins (clade I flavodoxins) may be important in oxidative stress response.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: A subset of flavodoxins (clade I flavodoxins) may be important in oxidative stress response.
source: Here we show that not all flavodoxins are responsive to low-iron concentrations, and that a subset of flavodoxins (clade I flavodoxins) may be important in oxidative stress response.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The specialization of flavodoxin clades might enable diatoms and other stramenopiles to survive in stressful rapidly changing environments.
source: This specialization might enable diatoms and other stramenopiles to survive in stressful rapidly changing environments.
evidence: This is a speculation about the ecological significance of the findings.

claim: The genetic duplication and functional differentiation of flavodoxin add a molecular mechanism that may facilitate diatom survival and adaptation to two major stresses – iron limitation and oxidative stress.
source: The genetic duplication and functional differentiation of flavodoxin described here add a molecular mechanism that may facilitate diatom survival and adaptation to two major stresses – iron limitation and oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.
